memory_versions.text:
Working notes — order intake validation

Form: v1 requires all six fields: cust, email, order_date, priority, qty, ship_country. All must be valid.

Process: each batch gets 3 attempts. Each rejection costs -0.20. After 3 rejections, the record goes to manual review and the next batch is assigned.

Observed ORD-5100–5109: all rejected. Most had 2 invalid fields; ORD-5104 had 1; ORD-5109 had 4. No successful intake yet.

Source records are unreliable: emailed pastes or phone-order transcriptions often appear as:
customer reads "Name"; did: {"cust":...,"email":...,"order_date":...,"pri...
They are frequently truncated or malformed, missing quotes/braces and later fields. The `did:` blob is not valid JSON as shown.

Do not trust front-desk notes to infer missing fields. Messages like “confirm details,” “ordinary priority,” “confirmation email,” or “duplicate check done” do not guarantee valid form data.

Likely invalid fields: absent/truncated priority, qty, ship_country; malformed JSON/braces. The prose name may be cut off, but the JSON cust can be fuller.

Before submitting: extract/verify all six fields. Require valid email pattern, ISO-like order_date, nonempty cust, valid priority, numeric qty, and ship_country. If any field is missing or unparseable, expect rejection. Preserve attempts for complete reconstructions.

Working notes — order intake validation

Form v1 requires all six fields valid: cust, email, order_date, priority, qty, ship_country.

Process: each batch gets 3 attempts. Each rejection costs -0.20. After 3 rejections, record goes to manual review and next batch is assigned. Confirmed through ORD-5119.

Observed ORD-5100–5119: mostly rejected. ORD-5100–5115 all rejected. ORD-5116 accepted on attempt 2 (+1.00). Many rejections report 1–3 invalid fields; ORD-5114 and ORD-5118 had only 1 invalid, so near-valid records occur. No clear field-count pattern from the prose note alone.

Source records remain unreliable. Emailed pastes or phone transcriptions often show truncated `did:` blobs, missing quotes/braces, and cut-off later fields. However, visible truncation does not prove the actual field is missing: ORD-5116 was accepted despite the displayed blob ending after order_date. Do not reject solely because the log truncates the JSON. Validate the full record when available.

Front-desk notes are not guarantees. “Confirm details,” “ordinary priority,” “confirmation email,” “duplicate check done,” “partner portal overnight,” and voicemail/phone source tags did not ensure validity. “Marked ordinary priority by the intake team” appeared on ORD-5116 accepted but also on ORD-5117–5119 rejected, so it is not sufficient.

Likely invalid fields: absent/truncated priority, qty, ship_country; malformed JSON/braces. Prose name may be cut off, but JSON `cust` is often fuller.

Before submitting: extract/verify all six fields when possible. Require valid email pattern, ISO-like order_date, nonempty cust, valid priority, numeric qty, and ship_country. If a known field is missing or unparseable, expect rejection. Preserve attempts for complete reconstructions.

Working notes — order intake validation

Forms v1 and v2 both list six required fields: cust, email, order_date, priority, qty, ship_country. Process unchanged: 3 attempts per batch; each rejection -0.20; after 3 rejections, manual review and next batch. ORD-5120–5129 all rejected; no v2 acceptance observed yet.

Front-desk notes are not guarantees. “Partner portal overnight,” “duplicate check done,” “confirmation email,” “ordinary priority,” “called to confirm,” handwritten/phone/voicemail transcriptions all failed. Treat them as context only.

Visible truncation is common but not proof by itself: ORD-5116 was accepted despite the displayed blob ending after order_date. Still, recent truncated records often fail: missing/cut priority, qty, ship_country, malformed JSON/braces. JSON `cust` is usually fuller than cut-off prose. Rejection counts can vary across repeated attempts on the same underlying record (Cy Sato: 3/2/3 invalid), so don’t overtrust the reported count.

Before submitting, extract and verify all six when possible: nonempty cust, valid email pattern, ISO-like order_date, valid priority, numeric qty, nonempty ship_country. If a known field is missing or unparseable, expect rejection. Avoid spending attempts on the same partial record unless you have a complete reconstruction; partial repeated records go to manual review.

Working notes — order intake validation

Forms v1/v2 require six fields: cust, email, order_date, priority, qty, ship_country. Process unchanged: 3 attempts per batch; each rejection −0.20; after 3 rejections, manual review and next batch. ORD-5120–5139 all rejected; no v2 acceptance observed yet.

Front-desk notes are never guarantees. Confirmed failures: "partner portal overnight," "duplicate check done," "confirmation email," "ordinary priority," "called to confirm," "marked ordinary priority by intake team," handwritten/phone/voicemail transcriptions. Treat as context only.

Rejections are consistently reported as "3 field(s) invalid." Pattern: when only cust, email, order_date are supplied (priority, qty, ship_country missing/truncated), the three missing fields are the invalids. Visible truncation of the source blob is common; a truncated record that omits priority/qty/ship_country should be expected to fail. ORD-5116 was accepted despite truncation, so truncation alone isn't proof — but partial reconstruction is.

Rejection counts vary on the same record (Cy Sato 3/2/3), so don't overtrust counts.

Repeated partial submissions on the same underlying record waste attempts and hit manual review: Cy Reyes (2), Dee Okafor (3), Cy Marsh (3), Bo Sato (2) — all lost to partial records.

Before submitting: extract and verify all six — nonempty cust, valid email pattern, ISO-like order_date, valid priority, numeric qty, nonempty ship_country. If any known field is missing or unparseable, expect rejection. Do not spend attempts on the same partial record unless you have a complete reconstruction; partial repeats go to manual review.
